utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Two matters. First of all, Mr. Galbraith, it turned out to be possible to move the Thursday afternoon session to the morning. I don't know whether we need that session at all. That's still to be seen, but at least it might accommodate some of your concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Further, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning you have your testimony, that is that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Then Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before Mr. Kehoe begins. I know you asked us yesterday to give us an estimate of time, and I'm glad that we have the morning session on Thursday. I would like to let the Court know based on reviewing after the Court session today and preparing today or yesterday and preparing this morning, I will probably -- two hours is a low estimate for me. It might be to two to three, and I wanted to make the Court aware of that, and we will do everything possible to make sure Mr. Galbraith can return home on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information, Mr. Kuzmanovic. As you know, the Chamber always before finally deciding the matter will consider how the time for cross-examination was used up till that moment. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, we left off yesterday talking just about some of the sequence of events prior to Operation Storm and even prior to summer 1995. And just based on your work in the area, the existence of the Krajina Serbs or the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina had a pretty dramatic effect on the country economically as well as security-wise, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you just elaborate on that just a bit?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was devastating economically. Croatia as we know is a spectacularly beautiful country with -- whose great asset is the coast with a place of natural beauty and also many historic monuments. The fact is the existence of this hostile entity for many of these years meant there were no tourists, no tourists at all. I remember my first trip to Split in July of 1993. Again, you couldn't drive there. You had to by boat, and we arrived in the city because the power lines were cut because the RSK held the dams. The city also didn't have power. It existed -- it had a hum of generators. So the impact was huge, and it was huge in other ways. Transportation, again, instead of being a short trip -- relatively short trip between two parts of the country. You had to take a long route. That obviously affected the shipment of goods. There was very high unemployment. Probably the best way to measure this would be to compare the per capita income in Slovenia to that of Croatia. In 1988, Croatia was probably 80 to 90 per cent of Slovenia. In 1994, probably it was - and here I'm just giving an order of magnitude - might have been 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was significant?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Huge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to -- and I turn to the second part of my question, the security concerns Croatia had with the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina on its border. Can you elaborate on that just a bit?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- until 1994 until the cease-fire there was regular shelling from the Serb-held territory onto Croatian territory. I would go down to Karlovac, for example, right on the front side -- or on the front line, almost a divided city, and occasionally shells would have landed there a few days before. I remember one trip, the church there had been hit a couple of times, and part of the -- I think it was the steeple had been knocked over. Zadar was right in range. Again, an important city. Beograd on the sea, a tourist destination. So not only were people at risk - not many people after 1991 were injured, but some were - but it's not very pleasant to live under that kind of threat, and of course for a place like Zadar or Beograd which depended on tourism, tourists just don't go to places that are being shelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and could you make a pause between question and answer, and then question again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Ambassador. I should have addressed that at the beginning, but since we speak the same language it is often difficult. Now to compound that problem in Croatia, prior to the events in July of 1995, there was a serious refugee problem, as well, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you talk to us about that a bit.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia was a country of four and a half million people. It had internally displaced Croats from 1991, I don't know, 2 or 300.00 people. Again, I wish I could remember the exact figures, and those people were put up in hotels along the coast. Actually, when I made my first trip there for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the Intercon at that time was one of the two premier hotels in Zagreb. Half of it was filled with refugees from Vukovar, which had just fallen, and those people were -- these Croats who had been expelled were in these coastal hotels for four years. Then in 1992, with the start of the Bosnian war, Croatia had - I don't know - I think a million more people come through into Croatia. Many of them went on to refuge other places, but it was a huge burden for a country this small. Croatia's record in terms of taking care of refugees wasn't 100 per cent good. There was some involuntary repatriation of Muslims to Bosnia, but it was extremely good. This was one of the truly admirable parts of what happened in the -- in those wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would include the treatment of both displaced Croats as well as Bosniaks coming through?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I think it's fair to say that the displaced Croats in general were treated better. They were after all citizens of the country, but the treatment of the Bosniaks was very good even during the Muslim-Croat war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you talked to us a bit about Mr. Babic yesterday as well as Mr. Martic, and in the -- if I can just go to this quickly. In your testimony in the Milosevic trial, you -- at page 32110, said: "For Martic" at line five: "For Martic it was" -- I'm sorry. 23 -- page 23110. You noted that for Martic it was absolutely out of the question. He said that Serbs repeatedly told me that Serbs and Croats could never live together, and if the area was integrated into Croatia that he would leave. Now he told you that there would be no reintegration into Croatia. That's an accurate assessment of your -- your position on your conversations with Mr. Martic, is not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel. I apologize for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to check the pages from the Martic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. It's 231 -- excuse me, this is from the -- I think it was Milosevic. Milosevic transcript. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I really insist on small pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies to counsel. It's Milosevic at 23110, line -- yes. Milosevic trial, that's right. Line 5 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your negotiations with the Krajina Serbs and with Martic, you noted in your statement - and I believe you have it before you, Mr. Ambassador; that would be your longish statement - you noted in paragraph 8 that the Krajina Serbs played endless games to avoid serious negotiations, and Martic seemed the main person behind these endless delays. Can you tell us a little bit about that, Mr. Ambassador, if you could, and maybe just pause -- let the folks in the booth catch up before you begin.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My involvement with this and what it was -- therefore was also the start of the so-called Z-4 process were cease-fire negotiations that took place in March of 1994 in Zagreb at the Russian embassy; there were two sessions. At the end of the second session, which concluded in agreement, the Serbs -- it was agreed that for the second set of negotiations which were going to be on economic- and confidence-building measures that they would begin in two weeks in Plitvice which was in Serb-occupied territory. And the Croats raised the issue of having Croatian journalists come to that event because Serb journalists from the Krajina had been covering the cease-fire negotiations in Zagreb, and the negotiator said, oh, yes; in fact, I was going to invite your journalists. The Croatians then submitted a list of five journalists that would accompany the delegation, not a large number for a country that had newspapers, radio, television. The Serbs rejected that because only two Serbs had come to Zagreb. That was largely because that was all the journalists they had, and on that basis this meeting didn't take place. The process didn't continue, and they played these kind of games endlessly because in my view they really were not prepared to face up to the issue, which is that there had to be a political settlement that would reintegrate this territory into Croatia. I did say that Martic was the -- I felt was the main actor. I felt that he had no interest in the well-being of the people of the Krajina region. I thought he was interested in himself, not very smart, and very much under the control of Milosevic, who, as I testified yesterday, put him into office. It may be that a more accurate statement would have been that Milosevic was really the main figure behind these delays because I'm sure if he had given the word to be Martic to be serious, then Martic would have managed to be serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned in the Martic case that when you were negotiating the Z-4 plan in January of 1995, Martic refused to even take a copy of the proposal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was the most extraordinary thing because you had the ambassadors of the United States, of Russia, of the -- I guess it was the French ambassador representing the European Union; you had a representative from the European Union itself and the United Nations, and they physically refused to touch a document that was a peace plan endorsed by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it Martic who refused to take it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic refused to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when your efforts, and I might say laudable efforts, in early August to late July to begin those last-ditch peace negotiations, you attempted to go to Knin to see Martic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reply came that I was unwelcome in Knin, and Babic then sent word that -- could I meet him in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you went to see -- you told us you went to see Babic in Belgrade, and he told you at that time that he was unable to -- or did he tell you at that time or thereafter that he was unable to meet with Milosevic concerning any of these peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that he was unable to meet with Milosevic and that one word from Milosevic and Martic would have accepted this package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back to your statement in paragraph 63, if I may. Mr. Ambassador, when you were attempting to broker this last-minute deal, you note that one word from Milosevic could have meant all the difference, but Milosevic did not meet with Rudy Perina. Now is who is that, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rudy Perina was the American charge d'affairs in Belgrade, so the top US official in Yugoslavia. We didn't formally -- we didn't recognise Serbia and Montenegro as a state, so we did not have an ambassador there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as part of your negotiations these first few days of August 1995, was it Mr. Perina's job to try to talk to Milosevic to get him on board?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But he was unsuccessful getting a meeting with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could not get a meeting with Milosevic on the 3rd of August, which was at a time it was apparent to everybody that military action was imminent. Military action that would very much affect the well-being of a significant Serb population that Milosevic himself had championed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just waiting a second. Now, based on this sequence of events, not only your inability to go to Knin to talk to Martic but the charge, Mr. Perina's inability to meet with Milosevic, what did you conclude?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that the prospects for a peaceful settlement were not good but that it was still very much worth pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Let me turn just a bit away from the Krajina Serbs and talk a little bit about the Republic of Croatia during this period of time and just walk through some of the peace initiatives that -- some of which you were directly involved in and brokered and -- such as the Vance Plan -- the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, most importantly the Washington Agreement. During the course of these various negotiations on these plans, did President Tudjman agree at your request to sit down and negotiate through all these plans that I just outlined and others?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So far as I know and think, he agreed to negotiate in every instance that he was asked to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a plan that you were heavily involved in, if I may, respectfully was the Washington Agreement in March of 1994. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit the Washington Agreement, and if you could just tell us a little bit about the background and what it did in your own words, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, full-scale fighting broke out between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia, and it was apparent to us that there was no prospect of ending the war in Bosnia as long as it was a three-way fight, and so our top priority - our being the US government, of course - was to end the Muslim-Croat war, and that involved getting a change of attitude from Croatia: First, in the atrocities to release the prisoners; and then to forge agreement between the two sides. That required a political settlement, and what we came up with on the -- at the suggestion, actually, of a part of the Bosnian Croats who were not aligned with the Herzegovinians, the Posavina Croats, was this plan for cantons, a federation -- a Muslim Croat federation in Bosnia-Herzegovina with different cantons, and that is what we negotiated in Washington at the very end of February and the beginning of March of 1994. Once that agreement was reached, the fighting between the two sides ended immediately, and they formed an alliance, and because of that alliance Bosnia and Herzegovina survived, and within 14 months or I guess 18 months, the war was over with a settlement that is far from perfect but a lot better than the continuation of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in your view, Mr. Ambassador -- so in your view, Mr. Ambassador, the Washington Agreement was a key ingredient to the ultimate bringing about of peace in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the cornerstone of the Dayton Peace Agreement. Had there been no Washington Agreement, I do not believe that Bosnia and Herzegovina would have survived, I don't think the Sarajevo government would have survived, and before he died I saw President Izetbegovic, and he said basically that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And President Tudjman on behalf of the Republic of Croatia went along with the Washington Agreement, did he not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not like the idea of the Washington Agreement. He did not want to conclude the Washington Agreement, but under intense pressure from the United States he was pragmatic enough to agree. At various times he did what he could to undermine the Washington Agreement, but in the end the agreement did survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, if we may, to a Prosecutor's Exhibit yesterday, 421. I don't know if you have it. We'll bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a P421 -- 451, excuse me. 451 is the excerpts from the "The United States and Republic of Croatia: A Documentary History." I don't if you have a hard copy before you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have the whole book here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, frankly, I don't want to read the whole book. I'm interested in the address or press conference you gave on the 2nd of June. It's page 91 of that document, yeah. It's the page -- the stamp -- the number on the top is 06069577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't appear on our screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can proceed. This is a P document, not a D document. P451.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not on the e-court screen. It is on my screen, as well, but it says -- no, there we are. Matter resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ambassador. Turning to the third-to-last paragraph beginning "Specifically," on the first page of that, and this is your speech on June 2nd, 1994. I'll read it as slowly as I can. "Specifically Croatia agreed to abandon the idea of a separatist Croatian republic in part of Bosnia and instead decided to support fully the territorial integrity, independence, and unity of that sovereign country. In doing so, Croatia put itself squarely on the side of international law and justice. Croatia's decision was key to the Washington Agreement, a political arrangement for a federation of Muslims and Croats with a governmental structure provided very substantial self-government for each community while fully protecting both the human and political rights of these communities." If you turn to the next page, fourth paragraph down, Mr. Ambassador, beginning with: "To reiterate ..." "To reiterate, the federation agreement would not have been possible without the fundamental shift in policy undertaken by the government of Croatia. When we talked to Croatia about becoming our partner in the peace process, we said that as our partner we would work through Croatia for its fastest possible integration into western political, economic, and security arrangements." Now, Mr. Ambassador, those were your words at that time after you had concluded the Washington Agreement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we move on, you were also brokering the Z-4 plan, and I think you told us yesterday that President Tudjman was not fully on board initially with the Z-4 plan, but he agreed to negotiate with the document that you presented him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not on board initially or ever. But he -- he did agree to negotiate on the basis of the document, and that was all that we asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that document carried with it the document you presented him substantial autonomy for the Serbs in the Krajina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very great autonomy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And can you explain that just a bit.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part of the Krajina, which had in 1991 a Serb majority, there would be a separate government with its own elected parliament, its own elected chief executive who would be known as the president of the Krajina. That government would have control over almost all government functions, police, education, culture. It could run its own welfare system, health system. It was entitled to fly its own flag along with the Croatian flag in the same way that, for example, an American state would -- has its own flag. The Krajina would be demilitarised, and we even allowed the possibility, and this was turned out to be quite controversial, that they could have their own bank-notes, much in the manner that Scotland has its own bank-notes even though the currency is the same as the pound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying with President Tudjman, and we don't need to go into tremendous detail. I mean, his negotiations continued through the Eastern Slavonia agreement, the Dayton Peace Accords, the Prevlaka Agreement, all of these agreements he and the Republic of Croatia continued to participate, did they not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the midst of this you were talking to Mr. Babic, and I think you said in your diary that notwithstanding your efforts in this regard, and I believe it's on July the 31st, on page 26 of your diary. On 31 July, you note that: "I point out that the Croatians have every reason to move militarily. The international community seems understanding. The Serbs are way off balance. They have parts of three brigades dealing with the Zepa remnants as they face a professional army in the west. It is sweet revenge on Mladic. Any negotiations now would be a stall." So as we move into this area, it was your conclusion at this point, Mr. Ambassador, that negotiations -- certainly the negotiations going on with Mladic's people in Geneva were a stall -- excuse me, Martic's people in Geneva were a stall?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that that is a reference to -- in fact, I will say that is not at all a reference to negotiations between Croatia and the Republika Srpska Krajina. It is a reference to negotiations in Bosnia, the ongoing contact group negotiations, which at that time as the momentum was beginning to shift from the Bosnian Serbs to the federation, I felt that negotiations after Srebrenica, after Zepa, would be a stall. But it -- this had absolutely nothing to do with the negotiations about the Krajina, and I think - and I could be wrong about that - but I think we did -- the September 3rd meeting -- the August 3rd meeting was not even set at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to this in a bit, though, but you did tell President Tudjman on the 1st of August during your meeting that you didn't hold out much hope for negotiations given all of the Krajina Serbs failures, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't at the moment recall whether I said that to President Tudjman, but I would not have had a lot of hope, and now that I think about it, it is possible that something along those lines were in my instructions. That is, in the demarche that I presented, but at this point right now I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You -- turning our attention to Geneva, you knew that you -- you were of the position that -- as with many others in the international community that those negotiations in Geneva were merely pro forma and that the Krajina Serbs were going to refuse every demand by President Tudjman, including the peaceful reintegration into Croatia. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that. I -- I thought that there was some prospect that Babic would be able to get the parliament to agree to accept the deal that I worked out with him on the 2nd of August. I wasn't sure of it, but given what I knew was going to be an enormous tragedy for the population of the Krajina, I felt that we ought to -- there ought to be a chance even of a few days to see if Babic could do what he promised he would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was talking about the meetings in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was linked to the Babic deal because what was supposed to happen was for Babic to speak to the representatives in Geneva and for them to publicly accept what Babic and I had worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, in the Milosevic transcript at page 23166, lines 5 to 14, you stated: "As to the meetings in Geneva, they, the Croatians, used them as a vehicle to present their final ultimatum. They anticipated that there would not be a positive answer, and they proceeded with their attack. I don't think the Croatians had the slightest thought that there was going to be meaningful negotiations, and it was clear to me, as it was to the other diplomats in Zagreb and I think to the broader international community, that the meeting in Geneva was just that, that it was pro forma, that it was a very dangerous situation, that Tudjman was going to outline demands that he had already stated, and that the Serbs were going to refuse them, and that that would provide the pretext for war." Did you state that during the Milosevic trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on this particular events or the sequence of events, starting with all of the negotiations with the Krajina Serbs, in paragraph 63 of your statement you note that there was a basis for the skepticism of the Croat leaders. "While I wish there had been more time, I also understood why there wasn't, and they were probably right to be skeptical." That was your ultimate conclusion, Mr. Ambassador, after you had finished all of these negotiations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that is correct. Just to come back to what I said in the Milosevic trial, it's certainly true that -- that what the Croatians envisioned that meeting to be a case -- a place where they would present demands which they knew would be rejected and so that that was not a negotiation. Nonetheless, as I was explaining, it did have a connection to the deal that I had negotiated with Babic, where if the Serbs accepted the deal with Babic or said they would, then it would be worth waiting a few days and see if they delivered on what they promised. But that wasn't how Croatia perceived that meeting. For them -- they didn't send their top negotiator. It was simply an occasion to present an ultimatum which the Serbs would refuse, and that set the stage for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the significant part of that demand that had always been the demand of President Tudjman was the peaceful reintegration into Croatia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the major demand, but in fairness to the Croatian position, the Serbs had not been forthcoming on a number of other measures, which they had previously agreed, which were much smaller like the pipeline and then reopening the connections through Krajina by rail and road so that the two parts of Croatia could be connected. So not only did they refuse -- were they not forthcoming on the big demand, but they hadn't been forthcoming on much smaller demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ergo your statement about the skepticism?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement about the skepticism -- the statement about the skepticism is more specific. It is -- it is that I believe the Croatians were right to be skeptical as to whether Babic would have the power to deliver on what he agreed with me. That -- in short that he would be able to overcome Martic. He said he could, but they were right to be skeptical as to whether he actually could overcome Martic and possibly or likely Martic and Milosevic. Again, I simply felt it was worth waiting a few days to see if that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us broaden the context of this and just talk about the larger geographic context in which you were attempting to negotiate this, and I'm talking about your -- you learning of the matters in Srebrenica and what was going on in Bihac and your reaction to that. Now, you touched on it briefly during the Prosecution's direct, and if you could just elaborate on that just a bit exactly what you were observing and what you were concluding based on the information that you were obtaining.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an extremely difficult time. The Serb forces had been on the offensive. They had taken Srebrenica. 7.000 men and boys were missing, and I was quite sure based on my own understanding of the region from serving two and a half years that in fact the missing were dead, so that I believe they were already dead. And then the attack on Zepa and the attack on Bihac. These attacks threatened to change the overall strategic situation in the -- in that part of the Balkans so that you would have a large west Serb state, including the Krajina and the Serbian parts of Bosnia. The position of this west Serb state would be much stronger militarily because once Bihac was gone they would not have to defend both sides of a donut. They would just have a single exterior border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The "they" that you're talking about are the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Continue.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. There was a humanitarian dimension. In Srebrenica there were 40.000 people, and Mladic had murdered 20 per cent of them. If he were to apply the same ratio to Bihac with 160.000 people, he would be murdering 32.000 people. It was unthinkable to me that that could take place in Europe 50 years after the Second World War and that the European powers and the United States would let that happen, but that was what we were afraid might happen. Then the whole UNPROFOR peacekeeping mission was in danger of collapse. The United States is a major part of the United Nations. We pay -- or at that time were paying 31 per cent of the costs, and our main allies - notably Britain, France, Spain, and others - had troops in the UNPROFOR mission that would have to be extracted by NATO. So this was an enormous crisis that was building, and my view was that if NATO was not going to save Bihac and it -- in its London statement, which I think was around the 22nd of July, it only mentioned Gorazde, not Bihac, and if NATO wasn't going to save Bihac, then -- and Croatia was willing to undertake military action that we should not object to that military action. That was my strong view, that was the position that I advocated to my government, and that was the position that my government took. As I wrote in messages, I -- I was aware that Croatian military action to save Bihac would produce a humanitarian crisis with regard to the Krajina, but in what I called the hierarchy of evils, the -- that humanitarian crisis clearly would rank lower than a situation which the Bosnian Serbs took Bihac and massacred 32.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I want to turn to a video to show you, and this would be 1D33009. This is a video from RSK TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before you play a video, I gave permission for two minors to be in the public gallery today for special reasons. I don't know what the video will show us, but I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's just a press conference, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- well, could I say that it is innocent or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, there's no expletives in there, nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, but I just wanted to be sure. That's -- it's my responsibility. So let look at the press conference, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] General Ratko Mladic, the legendary commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, an old acquaintance, and one of the Serb legends. This is therefore an opportunity to avail ourselves of the presence of General Mladic to address you and to ask him questions concerning the current situation which is of great importance to the Serb people. So I now give the floor to General Mladic. "General Mladic: Thank you very much. If I can take the opportunity to use the media in order to address the people -- to greet the people of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. We are here together. I have always been here even if I left and was away for a while, but I never really left. "Journalist: For starters, General, how do you perceive the situation as a whole in the Republika of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska? "General Mladic: I would say that the situation is currently rather complicated due to the comprehensive aggression carried out by the Croatian armed forces against the Republika Srpska, and the goal of their operations is to cut off the Republic of Serbian Krajina using their weapons and the mediators and pressure by the international community to enforce a solution in the area by means of force. But I hope that with the help of good organisation and the functioning of all the segments of the Serbian people in both the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the outcome will be resolved successfully, and I think that the Croats made a crucial mistake in this war which is going to cost them. "Journalist: Do the Serbs have enough strength to withstand the Muslim and Croat onslaught? "General Mladic: The Serb people have enough strength and enough forces, and had countries from the German and Islamic blocks not provided support, unfortunately, along with the support of some others, they would have lost this war long ago. Every prolongation of this war is catastrophic, first of all, for those who instigated it, and by this I mean the Croatian armed forces. "Journalist: General, from a strategic point of view, in my humble opinion, I think the Croat forces are very stretched -- stretched thin across the territory now and towards the Defence lines of our Serb defence forces. To what extent would that be helpful to our strategy for a successful strategic strike to retake and liberate our territories? "General Mladic: It's a good question, and you are displaying journalistic curiosity, but I wouldn't answer your question with any particularly high degree of certainty. Time will show, and time will answer your question. "Journalist: What is the current situation in the Grahovo and Glamoc theatres of war? "General Mladic: The Croatian army formations have attacked and have entered Grahovo and partially entered Glamoc, but I do hope we will retake these and other occupied territories of Republika Srpska very soon. "Journalist: Amongst other issues, we are interested in the situation in Grahovo and Glamoc and the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Numerous rumours are circulating among the public and even by some media in the Serb territories that there is insufficient defence coordination between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska. There are even rumours and attempts to bring unrest among the population. There are talks of some sort of selling out or surrender of our liberated lands for "greater gain." "General Mladic: First of all, I wouldn't wanted to comment on this calculated propaganda of a low intensity. As far as I'm concerned, the Serb populist is united from Kupa and Korana and all the way to Timok and south Morava rivers. I feel that the Serb people in those territories as all other peoples on this planet should have the same interest, the same state and remaining structures on such a state, and I believe that in this respect what's going on in every part of these territories, needless to say, and every individual on the planet that Serbs should be allowed to demonstrate an interest in at least the same degree as any other modern state demonstrates in its citizens living within their state or in foreign territory. "Journalist: We surprised you by his presence, but this doesn't mean that they haven't asked me many questions up to now. "General Mladic: You asked a good question. This isn't the first time the Ustashas are attacking, wanting to kill us. However, I believe the time has come that our people as a whole need to realise and which many have come to realise during this war and -- as I had indicated earlier. I believe terrible mistakes have been made by individuals who claim the war with the Croats was over once and for all and that it would be over within seven days, and then in the lines of separation numerous check-points were being opened, customs zones, and in some places there were even soccer games held. As you can see, these proved to be costly decisions resulting in the loss of lives, numerous refugees and burnt villages, but I hope that our people have understood this and that they have enough strength and that they will muster enough strength so that this aggression by Croatia and its armed forces during the whole time of this war in the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be avenged and that they will send them back to where they belong. "I just want to send my regards to the people to tell them that they should remain resolute in defending their country, their historic hearth and graves, and that they don't give in to our form of provocation or any form of propaganda because it is only with the means of our forces that we can create our state. A state can be made with its own children, and so many of our wonderful children have given their lives for both the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That should motivate the rest of us who are still alive and on our feet to apply additional efforts, and we should remain focussed on the finale of this war until the final victory. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, the unification of those RSK forces along with General Mladic was something that concerned you greatly, as it impacted not only on Bihac but on the rest of Croatia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Strategically, if I could just -- and I know you talked to us about the humanitarian fall-out. Strategically, what would have been the impact to Croatia had Bihac fallen with the Krajina Serbs and the Bosnian Serbs joining?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been a single western Serb state, which would have had a coordinated or united military command and which would have been defending only exterior borders. That is different from the situation that -- that would have -- that prevailed as long as Bihac was there where it was facing the Dudakovic and the 5th Corps from within Bihac occasionally attacking out and then lined up with Croatia on one side and the Bosnian army and the HVO on other sides. So the strategic situation for the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs would have been much better if Bihac had fallen. Now, this also concerned the United States because it would have meant that this war would have continued for a very long period of time, that once you had that entity created, the prospects for a piece negotiation based on what the international community had on offer, both for Croatia and for Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the contact group plan for Bosnia, the chances of achieving that would have been very small. So from Croatia's point of view, it would have been strategically disastrous, and from the point of view of the United States and our partners who were trying to make a just peace, it would have been a disaster as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just tender this video into evidence at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D402.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I know this video was talking about the fall of -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- admit it into evidence, it might be in your interest, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologize, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D402 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, I know that the video talked about the fall of Grahovo and Glamoc, but prior to that time you recognised this possible set of affairs that you have been talking about, and by the way, there was going be in your view a significant refugee fallout to compound the refugee fallout that Croatia was already dealing with, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my view that the 160.000 Bosniaks who lived in Bihac would have been -- the lucky ones would have been expelled, but it's likely that tens of thousands would have been murdered by Mladic. So it would have been both a big refugee burden to Croatia but also, you know, for the entire world and unspeakable mass murder, just like Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And to that end, Mr. Ambassador, you used your diplomatic efforts to push for the signing and execution of the Split agreement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Split agreement was an agreement between the government of Croatia and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The United States did not have any role in setting up the Split meeting, but the Croatian government asked if I would go down to that meeting, and I did. I think I actually was the only foreign diplomat; I and my staff were the only foreign diplomats to attend the meeting, and we -- I certainly encouraged the two sides to cooperate, and I suppose as a sign of our support for this agreement, when it came time to -- for the picture to be taken at the signing, Ambassador Zuzul one of the senior Croatian officials asked if I would be in the picture, and I agreed to be in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- let me bring up on the screen 1D33-0061. Mr. Ambassador, we're not going through this whole agreement, but if you look at paragraph 2, you know, it notes the attacks on UN Safe Areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the joint operations by Bosnian and Croatian Serbs against UN Safe Areas in Bihac. Mr. Ambassador, this agreement is in response to that, to allow the Croatian forces and the Bosnian forces to operate together in Bosnia to fight the Serbs, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the great significance of the Split agreement. It represented a request by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina acting consistent with UN charter with its right of self defence requesting the Republic of Croatia to provide assistance, and in that sense it was very different from the previous Croatian interventions in Bosnia. It was done in a lawful manner against a -- joint action against an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer 1D33-0061 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D403 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, it was your belief at the time that Croatia had potentially international border violations because ARSK soldiers were crossing from Croatia into Bosnia to fight. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of international law, a state has an obligation to prevent its own territory being used for attacks onto the territory of another state. The situation was somewhat complicated given that there was an UN presence, but nonetheless, yes, I thought Croatia had a -- there was -- had an obligation to make sure that there were not attacks from Croatia onto the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this agreement, Mr. Ambassador, was one of the objectives was to allow General Gotovina and the HV troops to launch what we call Summer 95 on Grahovo and other areas moving up from the Livno valley. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things that followed from the agreement was the offensive up the Livno valley, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on your time there, were those attacks successful in alleviating some of the pressure on Bihac?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were very significant and had a very positive effect of alleviating the pressure on Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me take you yet further. You knew that this agreement as well as the activities by General Gotovina and the HV were going to be the foundation for the ultimate taking over of the Krajina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes. I knew that this was part of a -- of a military plan that would involve taking over the Krajina. It didn't automatically follow that because of the Livno valley offensive that there would be an Operation Storm, but if there was to be an Operation Storm, this would -- this -- this operation would fit -- would fit into it. As I testified yesterday and in other trials, I was also aware of the planning for Operation Storm and the likelihood that it would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also knew that the fighting that potentially would take place through the taking over of Grahovo, for instance, and then -- taking over Knin, the ultimate goal would be the defeat of the Serbs, and the Serbs, I mean the joint efforts of the ARSK and the VRS. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia's ultimate goal, certainly, was to recover the Krajina region and I suppose to relieve the siege of Bihac and that -- and that this action would further that goal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when we are talking about -- I'm sorry. So when we are talking about the moving through on Summer 95 and as well as taking back the Krajina, it was also a desired effect for the Croats to defeat Ratko Mladic and the VRS army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly wanted Ratko Mladic and the VRS army defeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To that end?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we -- I mean, we welcomed the -- or welcomed in the sense of not publicly welcomed but were very happy to see the Livno valley offensive because it did defeat -- it was a setback to Mladic, and it helped relieve the siege of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To that end, Mr. Ambassador, what was required, based on your knowledge of the area at the time, to defeat General Mladic and his joint militaries -- the joint militaries of the ARSK and the VRS at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm going take your question in parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it required very much to defeat the military of the ARSK, but to defeat the military of the -- the Bosnian Serb army, I think there were two ways it could be defeated. First, by a NATO -- full-scale NATO intervention which arguably -- as authorised by the Security Council, which arguably should have happened but was not going to happen; or, in the alternative, by the combined forces of the Bosnian government and the HVO along with the Republic of Croatia perhaps supported by NATO air power. And that is, in fact, how the Bosnian Serb army was defeated, and that is what set the stage for the Dayton Peace Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these joint efforts that you are talking about that ultimately brought the Serbs to bear, you know now, Ambassador, were led by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to right after the Split agreement, if you will. I read your diary, Mr. Ambassador, and it appears to be quite pressured. If I may, if we can turn to - I don't know if you have your diary before you - the 24th of July. Let me just take you through some quotes on the 24th of July and the 25th. For your diary entry 24 July 1995: "War appears imminent. Croatians plan to move tomorrow at 4.00 on Bosanski Grahovo. The Serbs have artillery in Sector South and plan to retaliate by shelling Croatian cities. The Croatian plan would then be to take a sharp left at Grahovo and move into Knin," which is ultimately what happened with Operation Storm. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move to the 25th of July. The paragraph beginning: "I received a demarche." "I received a demarche from Bihac. I am instructed to deliver the demarche to the highest official." And then just for the sake of expediency, the last sentence, you give it to Ambassador Zuzul. "Zuzul understands its significance, that if Croatia behaves well it will not be punished for military action if through the Krajina to save Bihac." And now on the 28th, you receive notice that the combined forces -- meanwhile the HV and the HVO are about to take Bosanski Grahovo and Glamoc: "When I got back to the office, I learned that they had. We also have strong indications that Croatians intend an offensive to take all of Krajina." So as this multi-stepped process, you were following this along the way and discussing it with Croatian officials, and certainly with regard to the matters in the Livno valley you gave your approval to that on behalf of the United States?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A couple of questions there. Maybe they could be separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I -- I apologise for a multi-levelled question, Mr. Ambassador. Basically with regard to this process, you were following this on behalf of the United States, and in your discussions with the Croatian officials you were giving your approval for their activities going through -- up the Livno valley and taking Bosanski Grahovo in attempts of defeating the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs but also alleviating the pressure on Bihac. Is that a fair assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer it in part, first, yes, I was following this on behalf of the United States. Second, the United States was not approving of these operations in the sense of telling the Croatians to do this, but we were clearly not objecting, and in that context the fact that we were not objecting was highly significant because we and other countries had objected to any action that had expanded the war -- that arguably would have expanded the war, including objecting to military action, November 10th, 1994, during a previous Bihac crisis. So that was the significance, but I do not want to leave the impression with this Court that the United States was giving its stamp of approval to military action. We were simply not objecting. Obviously Ambassador Zuzul understood, and that's why I make the point in this thing that when I -- that -- in the diary that he understood that if Croatia behaved well, it would not be punished for military action. That is, there would not be sanctions, but that is a different statement from saying that there would be explicit approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I would like to turn your attention to an audio of part of your meeting with President Tudjman on the 1st of August. While we're coordinating that, we'll get back to that in a second, and I think the question, and you touched on it previously, was what was going on with the UN while you were present at the signing of the Split agreement and forces were joining together to fight the Serbs, and you were -- you had a degree of frustration with dealing wit the UN or the UN hierarchy during this time, wasn't there? Let me make this -- just direct to you a particular line in your -- might be easier just to direct you to your diary, June 12, lunch with Akashi and Janvier. "We got into a long argument about the UN role. Clearly is no humiliation. These two won't take. They are adamant against any use of force." Moving ahead to the 14th: "Fred Eckhart was showing Akashi his bad press." That's in the first paragraph, Mr. Ambassador. "He was particularly focussed on the Pomfret piece that said that the UN had abandoned its mission. I thought the piece had seemed quite accurate, and Akashi's case was not helped by numerous quotes from Sarajevo spokesman Ivanko." Let me just take a look at these two Pomfret articles, and then we can go back and ask questions in -- for the sake of moving more quickly, and if I could bring up 1D33-0076. And, again, Mr. Ambassador, this is a Washington Post article by John Pomfret, dated 11 June, 1995. And I won't read the whole matter, but as you can see under the body: "The UN mission here announced today that it will carry out no operations in Bosnia without the consent of the Bosnian Serbs, throwing into doubt its will to protect besieged Muslim enclaves and halt the shelling of Sarajevo." We can go to the bottom of the page of that article, starting with "Western sources": "Western sources said that draft security counsel resolutions circulating in New York and drawn up by France and Britain stressed that the UN mission in Bosnia..." If we go to the next page, please. Top of the page, please: "... must do only what the Serbs want it to and must abandon its threats to use force to protect Muslims." One more article, Mr. Ambassador. Bear with me, and we will ask a few questions about these in concert. And if I can bring up 1D33-0078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that you can deal with that in a couple of minutes so that we would have a break after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I -- I just go through this article, and we could take a break and, then I can just begin to question you after that. Satisfactory. Staying with Mr. Pomfret, Mr. Ambassador, this is an article in the Washington Post two days later basically talking about the same issue, and I want to highlight for you a quote on the second page. This is a quote, it is the second paragraph down, Mr. Ambassador: "'A lot of shots are being called by the Bosnian Serbs right now,' said Alexander Ivanko, the United Nations's top spokesman in Sarajevo. Asked if there were any -- if any were being called by the United Nations, he said: 'I can't think of any right now.'" When we come back, Mr. Ambassador, I would like to ask you a couple of questions about that, but at this time, Your Honour, I would like to offer into evidence those two John Pomfret two articles: 1D33-0076 and 1D33-0078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I saw that you have no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D33-0076 becomes Exhibit D404. 1D333-0078 becomes Exhibit D405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D404 and D405 is admitted into evidence. We'll have a break, but before we take the break I would like to deliver a very small decision. It can be done in open session. Mr. Galbraith, if you want to save ten seconds you're allowed to leave, but otherwise this is a corrigendum to the Chamber's decision on admission of the statements of seven witnesses pursuant to rule 92 quater issued on the 16th of June, 2008. On this 16 of June, the Chamber issued its decision on admission of statements of these seven witnesses pursuant to 92 quater. The Chamber has noticed that page 03070010 should have been included in the Roman numeral V in the disposition, and the decision is hereby amended to include that page. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on the matter. We will have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before we proceed -- Mr. Tieger, is there anything ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did have two quick matters, Your Honour, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you -- this is about cross-examination, so perhaps if you raise the issues you'd like to raise quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, yesterday we tendered bar table documents. I had a quick discussion with the registrar. We just wanted to make -- we thought perhaps those should be marked in advance. I know the Defence asked for time to review those, but in the meantime perhaps those could be marked. And secondly, yesterday a document was presented, a map, that was labelled as borders according to the signing the memorandum, the Academy of Arts and Sciences. I had an opportunity to check that document; couldn't find a reference there that would be -- that I understood to give rise to that map, so I would grateful if my learned friend at some point could point to the portion, and we can work with that out of court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I might add that the witness said that he didn't know for sure, so I didn't offer that document -- that map at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would know you had asked us as soon as we had a chance to offer thoughts on the bar table documents, and I wanted to do that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have had a chance to look at at least the first third of them, and for the most part we don't have any objection. But the very first document, the 65 ter 3209, we do object to because it's a 1992 meeting relating to population transfers and discussions between Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats, which we believe is not relevant to this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you at least for giving us already an impression about your position in relation to those documents. As far as the bar table documents are concerned, I suggest to the parties that I invite already the registrar to assign numbers to them so that they are marked for identification, and then the decision will follow later. But apart from that, Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber has carefully considered the course of the cross-examination until now. The Chamber has observed how the background of Operation Storm has been explored in great detail, including political, strategic, and tactical aspects of the events leading to Operation Storm. The Chamber does not ignore the relevance and importance of that background but also considers that this relevance and importance is not without limits. The Gotovina Defence has announced that it would need six hours of cross-examination of Mr. Galbraith. Having considered the course of the examination until now, the Chamber considers that it would be fair to limit the Gotovina Defence alone to the same number of hours as the Prosecution used. That would be two hours and 49 minutes. The Chamber, however, decided that it should grant the Gotovina Defence five hours in total for cross-examination. Further, the Gotovina Defence is encouraged to avoid repetition, to use its time in a focussed way, and to come to the relevant points as directly as possible, and to find a fair balance between the background of Operation Storm and the core issues of this case, that is, whether or not crimes were committed and to determine whether the accused bear criminal responsibility for such crimes, if any. This decision exclusively deals with the time for cross-examination of the Gotovina Defence. The time requested by the other Defence team seems at this moment in time not reasonable, but the chamber reserves its final position after it has had an opportunity to see how the cross-examination by the other Defence teams develops. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I want to bring up one other item before I ask you some questions in this regard, and if I could take a -- bring up 1D33-0068. This is a quote that -- from a book called "Complicity With Evil," Mr. Ambassador, and I want page 128, page 4 of that, which has been loaded up. And I'm looking at the quote portion on the bottom of the page, Mr. Ambassador, and onto the next page. If we could just go up a little bit more. The quote starts actually: "'The United Nations had a whole collection of reports of atrocities, and this was just one more of them,' recalls Galbraith, 'but we knew 7.000 people were missing, and this was proof of what happened to them, which I suspected from the start. I was sure that it would be buried by the United Nations. In Akashi's world, the reaction to something like this was that the United Nations had to be careful because it was dangerous and could lead to military action. The United Nations always needed proof, and they had strategies to ensure there was no proof. They would sit on reports or ensure the information was not highlighted, and when it was reported by the press, it just became part of more of the same from Bosnia. But for me, this was a flash message, that this massacre had happened.'" Now, Mr. Ambassador, I know there are several ideas here going from June into the discussion of Srebrenica and Zepa. But if you could tell me, I mean, what was going on with you coordinating with the UN throughout June and July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked before, and then when you -- you then presented the material. You asked if I was -- if I had disagreements with the United Nations, and needless to say I had strong disagreements with the United Nations and was very frustrated with how it was conducting itself, particularly in those months, and I think the -- the comments that you have quoted from my diary speak for themselves, so I don't think I need to elaborate on that unless you would like me to. I think I need to say something about this particular quote that you have raised from the Adam Labore book about what happened. The United Nations had -- because it is so significant and so representative. The United Nations -- you had had the Srebrenica massacre and after -- sorry, you'd had the fall of Srebrenica and then the women and children were brought by bus to Tuzla, and at that time that was the -- what the world was focussing on were the human rights violations for those women and children. The UN had people who were interviewing then. And then came this man who was a survivor of the massacre, and he described being taken to -- I won't go into detail, but being taken to a mass grave, shot. The bullet grazed his head, and he climbed out of it and made his way through the woods. And this was just taken down as another report, and when it got back to Zagreb, to the UN headquarters, one of the UN officials was very concerned that it would just go into a drawer and that -- and the reaction there was, We need more proof, and so she shared it with me, and I then sent a message saying, This is what's happened to the men and boys. But to me, this was simply proof of a massacre and it was -- which -- in circumstances where other people were in peril, namely the population of Bihac. This is the 25th of July. And so, yes, you could say that I was frustrated and had differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was a position of the UN that you note in your diary there, adamant against any use of force. Now during this period of time, was it your conclusion the UN simply was not going to use any force to assist in resolving the matter in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the assignment of the United Nations, and the -- and -- to give the United Nations credit, the humanitarian efforts that it ran kept hundreds of thousands of people alive and if it hadn't been for the UN, Sarajevo, for example, would not have survived. But -- and it was under-resourced and you had peacekeepers in blue helmets in the middle of a war zone, so -- and a final point is there were not American troops there, so it was a touchy matter for the American ambassador to be talking about this. Nonetheless, it failed in its mission to protect the safe areas and to stand up against the Bosnian Serbs, and it was also very unwilling to authorise NATO air-strikes, which was authorised by the Security Council, but it required -- before they could take place there were two keys -- the UN had to approve and the NATO had to approve, and it was very hard -- the UN was reluctant to turn its key. It always insisted that the United Nations was somehow neutral, but that in fact was not true. The United Nations was not neutral in this conflict because it had passed more resolutions on the former Yugoslavia than on any other conflict, and every single one of them identified Serbia as the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it your conclusion at that time, Mr. Ambassador, that the United Nations was not going to use force to prevent the fall of yet another UN protected area, that is the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- yes, it was my conclusion that the UN troops there were not going to defend the pocket because, after all, the Dutch troops had not defended Srebrenica, and the troops in Bihac were less capable. But it was also my conclusion, and this is much more relevant, that they were not going to turn the -- they were not going to authorise the NATO air-strikes that might have saved Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us if we can just at this point, we can tender that portion of the -- of the book, 1D33-0068.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D406 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I want to move ahead to the events beginning just the days prior to Storm, and just as a reference point. We talked about this before in your diary of the 31st saying that any negotiations was now -- would now be a stall. But I would like to play you a tape of your meeting with President Tudjman, and if I could bring up 1D33-0439. Just for reference points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the 1st of August on Brioni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour. I'm not sure how much of the tape will be played. What I've had a chance to review based on the portion that was disclosed appears to a smallish excerpt, so I leave it to the witness, of course, in terms of ability to contextualise this, but many of the portions are small fragments of what are obviously longer meetings, so two things: The extent to which the witness may need to see more of the transcript or the recording of the meeting; and secondly, we would need to receive the full transcript or recording of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We in fact gave the full tape to the Prosecution. We are not going to play each and every item in this take just for the sake of time. We're going to play about three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you will tender the whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just going to tender the portions, Your Honour, that I'm going to play. I had given the entire tape of the meeting to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will listen to it and see whether the Chamber needs any further context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Tieger, if you would have any suggestions what would be needed to get the proper context, then of course you're free to address the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Galbraith: The military intervention in the Livno valley has in fact had the desired effect. It's relieved the attack on the Bihac pocket and has put new pressure on the Serbs. But as you know, we remain extremely concerned the about the risk that any -- that continued offensive action by your forces could lead to a dangerous escalation in the conflict, and frankly what they mean there is action in Croatia, that is across the cease-fire line. I don't think there's any -- this is not aimed at the Livno valley offensive. We're concerned that there's a real danger of a Serb overreaction as there is of bringing together the Croatian Bosnian Serbs along with the FRY and an even more hard-line alliance. Zuzul has minimised the chances of a direct Yugoslav intervention, but we think that the dangers are greater than what he says, and so our advice is to be careful in avoiding escalating hostilities unnecessarily and to explore whether the events of the last few days can lead to a reinvigoration of the search for negotiated solutions. Today, however, we see little sign that the Serbs are withdrawing from their siege of Bihac; little sign that they are honouring previous agreements, that is the oil -- opening the oil pipeline; little sign that they are engaged on the issues that you have raised, opening the railroad connection or beginning negotiations on political summit; and little sign that they're prepared to allow UNCRO to exercise its full mandate; and if so we have no immediate optimism about negotiations on a political settlement. Nevertheless, we urge to you leave the door open for talks. Serbs and their leaders need time to face the new realities. And in this regard, depending on what you tell me about your plans and how you feel about it, Babic has sent a message to me through Akashi that he would like to see me in Belgrade on Thursday or Friday, and it would all -- whether I would do this or not would depend in good measure how you felt about and also what you tell me about what you're planning to do."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is just one part of the a conversation. We'll get into the next part setting out exactly what you -- the United States government's position is on whether or not the Krajina Serbs are willing to negotiate at this point. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the -- the tape speaks for itself. I -- I want to be clear, though, that what's being talked about here, which is in a demarche from Washington that I'm -- that is in a written form, and I'm talking about that demarche, and I'm then handing it over to Tudjman, not all of which necessarily reflects my own views. That is different from the negotiations that I was referring to on the previous day in my diary, which did reflect my own views when I was talking about a stall. That was about Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll just play the -- well let's play the next portion of this tape, which is 1D33-0080.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Galbraith: I want to -- just to reiterate some of the points that we've made before, which I know many of them reflect your policy, but I would not be doing my duty if I didn't restate them. First, to make clear, you know, it is our advice against military action, and we're not in any sense giving you a green light as some people say in the press. Second -- "Tudjman: We didn't say. "Galbraith: Yeah, I know. No, I know you didn't. I know you didn't, but, you know, this is around -- but I want to be clear. Second, I know -- you don't need our advice on the risks. You've made your own judgements, but should things not turn out the way you hope they turn out, you cannot expect that we will come in to the rescue. I think you understand that. Third, the treatment of the Serbian population in any area you take is extremely important, frankly, although Western Slavonia was not perfect. There were problems. The -- "Tudjman: But minor problems. "Galbraith: The reflectively good and certainly relative by this conflict treatment of the population and behaviour earned you enormous credit, and I think this was a major factor in international acceptance or the low level of the international reaction. You will -- under these circumstances, in any statements we make we will always emphasise the problems because it's impossible to ever know that there were not problems, and we are always going to be concerned about the problems, but it -- we did notice how much better this was than some of the other things like Medak and -- but we just want to emphasise so strongly that how important this is, that -- that the troops behave well if they do anything. It is also an obvious point, I know you appreciate, that troops that treat civilians well also turn out to be troops that fight better. I mean, they -- I suspect when you take on -- well, you have been taking on rapists, murders, and torturers in Bosnia, and they don't fight very well. They're quite good when they're dealing with 14-year-old girls, but not when they're dealing with a professional army. Finally, it is of paramount portion that any action be taken in a way to -- that there be no UN casualties. We know that there are UN -- the Serbs have put tanks next to some UN observation posts. Even if those tanks fire on you, it is critical that you not fire back. This will be something -- this involves our allies, and this is an absolutely critical point. "Tudjman: In such a case, in such a case our units don't fire such point, but ... [indiscernible] "Galbraith: No, I know that you have already considered these points. Again, let me emphasise it is our strong advice against doing this, but you've seen over the three demarches I have presented what our full position is. "Tudjman: Yes, I know. I quite understand. "Galbraith: I -- I know."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
