utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, talking about this a bit, you talk about a contrast between what happened in Operation Flash and Medak pocket and how -- I believe you said that what happened in Western Slavonia earned you tremendous credit in the international community or words to that effect. What exactly was going on there, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia, a part of the population remained. It was protected. We were working with Croatia to try and persuade these people that they had a future in Croatia after Operation Flash. There were also aspects of the Western Slavonia operation that involved human rights violations. I think some I may have become aware of were more focussed on after this conversation, and I may have overstated the case when I said that you earned enormous credit with the international community for what -- how east -- western Slavonia was handled. At least I feel listening to this 13 years later that I overstated the case. Nonetheless, in Western Slavonia about 3.000 of the population remained. They stayed in their homes. You didn't have the kind of burning and looting that characterized what happened in the Krajina, and it was really -- my point was to try and get Croatia to respect the rights of the civilians, and that was a point that I made to Tudjman in -- in other encounters, and also this was at the Villa Weiss [phoen]which is where he had meetings - I guess actually where he stayed, as well - on Brioni. So I would -- not all the conversation with him would have taken place in the recorded formal session. I would have also been making these points separately, as well, during that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to a document, and it is a 65 ter 3132, which is just one day after -- it not in your book, Mr. Ambassador. If I can bring it up on the screen. This is one day after your meeting. This is a meeting, Mr. Ambassador, at the Minister of Defence. If we could turn to the third page of that document. I mean, just if we -- that's right. If we could just look at this briefly. This is a meeting chaired by Minister Susak with various officers present and other members of the Ministry of Defence, and of course we see at 25 is General Gotovina. And if we can turn to the third page of this document, and -- at the Minister Susak aspect talking to the -- about midway through that interlineation, Mr. Ambassador: "Military police must be more energetic in its actions and must prevent all offences. ZP commanders" -- military district commanders -- "must be the ones to pass on to the other commanders the prohibition of any kind of uncontrolled conduct, torching, looting, et cetera. We must prevent having to take the heros of the home land to Court. PD" -- ideological and political workers -- "must carry out their task of appropriately briefing HV members. "The west has given a partial blessing but nothing must happen to UNPROFOR." I'd like to talk to you that in conjunction with one other document that's already been received in evidence, and that is D201. This is a -- part of the general attack order from General Gotovina, and if we turn to the second item, 6 -- excuse me, next page 6. It is page 2, item 6, I'm sorry. If we can just blow up 6 and 8 a bit. As I noted, this likewise is a day after your meeting with the president, Mr. Ambassador. This is also dated the 2nd of August. An order goes out: "Familiarizing units with the need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface in the course of combat operations with a focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns." "8. Advising members of units on conduct with civilians and POWs in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Turning my attention to these two documents, Mr. Ambassador, was this the type of reaction that you expected that the government of Croatia would have to the demarche that you presented or requirements that you presented to President Tudjman on the 1st, orders such as these?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's only too bad it didn't turn out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this is what you -- this is the kind of order that you were looking for to being passed down by someone like General Gotovina before this enterprise was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offer into evidence -- excuse me, we also tender the audios. 1D33-0439, 1D33-0080, and 65 ter 3135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, first the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection to the audio, Your Honour, with the reservation that to the extent any additional portions may also be tendered in -- to accompany that. Certainly no objection to that excerpt. And no objection to the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Transcripts have been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I listened rather than looking at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transcripts are there. Mr. Registrar, for the first audio -- or would you like to have them together, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it might be easier just to do them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two audios, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Separate. I take that back, Judge. I'm being told separately is much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 1D33-0439 becomes Exhibit number D407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D407 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D33-0080 becomes Exhibit D408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D408 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter 03132 becomes Exhibit D409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the number you just read is not exactly the same number as Mr. Kehoe unless there's any problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I made a -- incorrect. I mentioned the number as being incorrect. I think it's 65 ter 3132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3132 where the -- yes, you corrected that. Yes. I had overlooked that. D409. Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D409 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in other contexts, and I address ourselves to the Milosevic transcript at 23 -- 23169. You mentioned that -- at line 18 to 20 in talking about this entity known as MPRI. I know you're familiar with that. An MPRI was an entity that came and trained the Croatian armed forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It provided assistant -- certain kinds of training to the Croatian armed forces. It did not provide military training in the sense of -- or combat training. In other words, it operated in a manner consistent with the arms embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was part of that training as you mentioned in the Milosevic case training on human rights?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, moving ahead, you mentioned also in your conversations with President Tudjman that in addition to safeguarding civilians there was also a request that nothing happen to UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And consistent with that, nothing did happen. There were some event -- accidents, but nothing happened to attack individual UN conclaves or entities, did it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a Danish sergeant killed around Petrinja, but that may have been by the Serbs. I don't remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you -- I wouldn't mind even if you would tell us because apparently everyone understands but, the MPRI, isn't that an entity that came -- from where it did come?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was a -- well, maybe we just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You could ask the witness, but it's totally unclear to the Chamber where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, can you just elaborate on that just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not -- if you say this was -- from what country they came, by whom they were sent, that's good enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think a little bit more explanation. It is an American private organisation made up of former US flag officers and others which provided training under contract to third country militaries, and it would have -- it would have -- in order to do it, it had to get a licence from the state department, but it was a private contract between Croatia and this company, private company based in, I think, Alexandria, Virginia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, you put forth these requests, and there was some discussion as to whether or not there was a green light and a red light or a yellow light. The fact is that as far as the United States government was concerned, there was no light, is that right, to go attack the Krajina or not? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Court has just heard exactly what I said to President -- or at least one of the thing -- a principled point that I said to President Tudjman on instructions about it, so I'm not sure that -- that the lights are really all that helpful. We certainly didn't say, don't do it, and we didn't say, do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention just briefly to 65 ter 5230, which is your interview with Mr. Engel and Mr. Goldman.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And page 8. The bottom of that page we are talking about this, and you were asked: "Would you describe it as an amber light, a precedent?" And this other individual, Mr. Engel, says: "A little unprecedented time." And you note: "Oh, it was no light, but it was no light, but it -- no light was understood to mean a green light."

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croatians did go ahead, and they understood that we weren't saying no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did they also understand based on your conversations that if they did go forward that there wouldn't be sanctions as long as they abided by the requirements that you set forth in your conversation with President Tudjman on the 1st?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure they understood that, and that was something that we would have wanted them to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we will offered into evidence 65 ter 5230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what are we -- the whole of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's an interview, Your Honour, just -- the whole of the document was a 65 ter document. Just -- it puts the matter in context. It goes on for a few pages. I think it would be difficult to -- I think it's only 14 pages with the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we know by now who Mr. Engel and Mr. Goldman are?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can ask that. I'll ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes because we get an interview. We don't know if it is a press interview or for anything else. I would not mind -- I mean, if the parties know both who Mr. Engel and Mr. Goldman are. I'm not as formalistic as that we should hear from Mr. Galbraith. I'm certain that he'll jump up if you give the wrong information, so if you just tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tell you, Judge. They are two United Nations employees that were -- they were not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: State Department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: State Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are jumping up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: State Department employees. I apologize.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. They were -- there was a contract project to write a history leading to Dayton that was -- it was actually a classified history initially, and so they conducted interviews. They may have been under contract to the State Department, so they may not be State Department employees. I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is clear to me. Please proceed. But of course at the same time you'd like to hear a decision. No objections by the Prosecution. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D410, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D410 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead, Mr. Ambassador, you knew that that -- after your conversation with President Tudjman on the 3rd that the HV was going to move ahead with the attack, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yet you also mention in paragraph 30 of your statement that -- in talking about President Tudjman, he was generally cautious on the use of force. And, again, on -- in paragraph 63 you note in the middle of paragraph 63, when you are talking about your conversation with President Tudjman after your discussion with Babic: "Tudjman had been cautious and reluctant about the use of force, and some of that is reflected in the fact that Tudjman devoted time before Operation Storm to meet with me and then met with his advisors to consider the discussion before deciding on war. The fact that they listened to me reflects their inherent caution." Talk to me a little bit about this caution, Mr. Ambassador, at this particular juncture.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tudjman had lived through the Second World War, and so he knew what war was about. He was somebody who very much had the interests of Croatia as he saw it at heart, and in that sense I distinguish him from Milosevic, who I think had his own personal interests at heart, so a decision to go to war is one that he and frankly the other people in his government would weigh carefully. I don't think there were any -- or at least there were not many trigger-happy people among those senior leaders. I cited Tudjman as cautious because a very similar set of issues arose in November of 1994 in which Granic and Susak asked me what the US attitude would be if Croatia launched military action through the Krajina to relieve a siege of Bihac that was going on at that time. And I got instructions to say that we -- we -- we advise strongly against doing that. And when I delivered that response, Tudjman said, Well, I agree with you in the presence of Granic and Susak, and so I think that reflected his caution. And in the build-up to Operation Storm, he wanted to be sure that Croatia was not going to end up isolated from the international community, that the Security Council would not condemn Croatia, the Security Council wouldn't impose sanctions. Like any good strategist, frankly, he wanted to consider all the consequences of what he was going to do and in every way minimise the risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know you -- I'm sorry. I know that you didn't know about those -- I'm sorry. I know that you had seen some of those Ministry of Defence documents from the 2nd of August as well as General Gotovina's -- excuse me, order on that same date. But does that reflect a melding of that caution to try to ensure orders go down and people were taken care of and that UN personnel was taken care of?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the attack itself. If I can just address you to paragraph 59 of your statement, sir. You note in the first line that: "My impression was that the initial phases of the operation were relatively respectful of international law such as bringing people to camps where I understood they were not abused. The Serbs were confined" -- excuse me. "Serbs confined in camp did criticise the shelling to which they were subjected, but this was an indication that they could speak freely. The systematic destruction of Serbian homes and the killing of stragglers, et cetera, built up over time in the weeks after Storm." In paragraph 43, you talk about the actual -- I won't read the whole item, but you talk about the shelling of Knin, that it was not indiscriminate. You noted based on conversations with your attaches it was consistent with what you might expect and not indiscriminate. So it was your conclusion that the actual attack in Operation Storm in these first few days was consistent with international humanitarian law. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were major violations of international humanitarian law in those first few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is the operation that was conducted under the command of General Gotovina. You know that now.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just stand with -- with that statement. At this point, and this is many years, I don't want to be in the position of imputing knowledge that probably I had then as to who was in command of what operation. I principally dealt with President Tudjman and Defence Minister Susak, and so I don't want to -- I don't want to talk specifically about what General Gotovina was doing at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Staying -- going on to paragraph 44, you talk about your -- Colonel Leslie's observations. You say: "I understand that Colonel Leslie of UNCRO made observations that are inconsistent with this view, but I would express some scepticism about those observations. I also tried to -- I also recall that I tried to warn Colonel Leslie that the operation was about to stop but that my warnings were ignored." Tell me about those skepticisms, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, the UN - and I think this was significantly based on Colonel Leslie - asserted that there was indiscriminate shelling of Knin. But the UN personnel including Colonel Leslie were basically locked down in the UN headquarters. Because of our close relationship with the Croatian government, we had access that the UN did not have to Knin in the immediate aftermath of -- and to the Krajina in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm, and so I myself travelled into the Krajina region, and people from the embassy travelled, and that included our defence attache and the people in the defence attache's office as well as political office -- officers, Tim Knight, the DART team when it was there, so we had military, political, humanitarian. I'm just trying to give you the scope of the coverage so that I can then give you the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just -- I know it's an acronym, but was is DART?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Disaster Assistance Relief Team. This was the major US humanitarian operation in the former Yugoslavia, and it was run out of our embassy. In any event, so we had -- we had people there I think on the 7th and 9th of August looking at what had happened in Knin, and all of them reported to me that -- that the -- that the damage from the shelling was not extensive, in fact, that -- that things were largely undamaged and that windows were broken, that short of thing had happened, but there was no -- there was not a kind of systematic effort to destroy Knin. And I would distinguish the shelling of Knin from the other kind of shelling that took place in the war; for example, the shelling of Vukovar, the shelling of Sarajevo which did not take place in the context of a military operation to take a specific objective but which was stand-off shelling aimed at destroying the place, and in the case of Vukovar, destroying it before taking it. It was not that kind of shelling, and it was nothing like -- the damage was nothing like the damage that was inflicted on Dubrovnik, which also took place in a very short period of time, a few days in 1991, which I myself was an eye-witness to because I was there about ten days later. So that -- it is on the basis of that -- of the observations of the embassy -- of these three different embassy staff teams with three different functions including military experts who had a lot of familiarity with what was going on in the -- in the war who had been following it for years. It is -- it is their expertise as well as my own observations and when I went to Knin much later that led me to be skeptical of this claim of kind of -- of massive shelling, which is what I understand Colonel Leslie to have been saying after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the cable that you were mentioning, if I can just put that in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can bring up D66.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May have been some time since you laid eyes on this, Mr. Ambassador, but it is a cable of -- dated 14 August. It notes in the first paragraph: "None of the Serbs who spoke with us complained of mistreatment by Croatian authorities, and government of Croatia civil authorities have taken great pains to demonstrate publicly their commitment to protect Serb and Serb property." Next to the bottom of that page on the downtown Knin: "Although Knin was reportedly heavily shelled in the early hours of the hostilities, few downtown buildings and residential areas showed signs of shell damage. You talk about the -- go two pages up, please. "Conditions at the government of Croatia-controlled camp were better, where about 250 Serbs were living in a school gymnasium. All had a roof over their head, and most had mattresses. Government of Croatia officials had provided them with three meals a day and had trucked in sufficient water." This was the information you were getting from your representatives on the ground. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of three teams that went there, and there are actually three cables reporting on it. One a defence department cable, one from the DART team, and this from the political team, and they -- with regard to the shelling they all come to the same conclusion and also with regard to many of the other observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I move back, Mr. Ambassador, to P451 that talks about your -- this is a news conference that you conducted with Secretary Shattuck, if I may, on September 30th, 1995. I think it is in your book, Mr. Ambassador. Do you see that, sir? It has the number on the top. It's 244. The excerpt is -- the number on the top is 06069773. It's a press conference that you gave on September the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The ERN is 06069735. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, this is a press conference you gave with Secretary Shattuck on the 30th. And, if I may, go to the second page. On the top of that page, you note at the top of that page with Secretary Shattuck -- and this is a press conference you gave about the problems that were taking place in the Krajina, and you note: "First, we have -- are receiving continued reports of major human rights abuses that have occurred in the Krajina region following military action by Croatia in early August. These include killings of ethnic Serb civilians, particularly the elderly, after the Croatian home guards moved in. Beatings and other physical violence against ethnic Serbs, mass burnings and lootings of Serb houses and property."

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is not me who is saying this. This is it Secretary Shattuck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, going back to your particular statement in paragraph 59: "The systematic destruction of Serbian houses and the killing of stragglers, et cetera, built up over time in the weeks after Storm." So in your mind, Mr. Ambassador, the initial operation to take the Krajina was relatively, according to your testimony, in accordance with international law, but these other matters happened down the line after home guards moved in. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my -- my testimony is that the initial -- there were not major violations of international humanitarian law in the initial phases of Operation Storm, and subsequently there were major violations of international humanitarian law which included the systematic destruction of Serbian homes, mass -- mass looting, and the killing of stragglers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, these other individuals that were doing this, do you have any knowledge whether or not -- any particular unit they belonged to, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. "Other individuals" seems to be a reference to somebody or some bodies that are not referenced in the previous answer that I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individuals that were conducting these activities, do you have any knowledge what units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage, I -- I do not, and my -- my view of this was very straightforward. I considered the -- President Tudjman and the Croatian leadership responsible for -- for either permitting this activity to take place, which I considered to be preventable, or possibly having even ordered it. But I am -- I am not taking a position, and I certainly at this point could not, as to which Croatian units were responsible or who below the level of -- of President Tudjman and I suppose the defence minister might have been responsible for these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to any of these individuals, be they part of a HV unit or not, I mean, are you aware of any efforts that took place within the Republic of Croatia to try to get this matter under control such as, for instance, to mobilising 70.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such as demobilising them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Demobilising them.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the demobilisation was a matter of -- I mean, the troops were called up in a relatively brief period of time in preparation for Operation Storm, and then once Operation Storm was over, this massive conscription in a small country, it was natural that the troops would be demobilised, but I certainly did not see the demobilisation as being an effort to gain control over the Krajina or to prevent looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And more specifically, Mr. Ambassador, do you know of any efforts by the Republic of Croatia to try to get this matter under control?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that they took sufficiently serious steps to bring this matter under control because it is my belief that the top Croatian leadership in fact was quite happy that the Serb homes and property were destroyed so that Serbs could not return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, the question was whether you specifically know of any efforts. Your answer was about beliefs, and you repeated what you said earlier, but Mr. Kehoe is apparently seeking your knowledge about specific actions. May I -- you have noticed that Mr. Kehoe is limited in his time. Could I ask you to carefully listen to the question and to try to answer them as precisely as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not now know of specific efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ambassador, to follow up on your prior answer concerning the mobilisation, this massive mobilisation that you discussed prior to Operation Storm and then the demobilisation, this was of soldiers who were not professional soldiers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me turn topics to -- just for one moment, and you noted for us before that -- I'm not going to go back to it, but that Martic did not want to -- wouldn't agree to a peaceful reintegration, but I want to talk to you about the Serbs actually leaving. And if I can turn my attention to your diplomatic diary first, and I'll talking about the 15th of June, towards the bottom of the page, and this is on page 14. Do you see that Mr. Ambassador? "If Croatia took the territory."

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. You note on the first line: "If Croatia took the territory the Krajina Serbs would leave." Moving ahead in your diary to the 2nd of August, you're chronicling your conversations with Mr. Babic, and on page 30 of your diary when you're talking about the attack -- I'm sorry, I don't want to get ahead of you.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. You note -- you've told Babic that if it goes the people will flee and that the problem would be if there was a war and people left. And lastly, if I could just go to a video, 1D33-0088 -- it is 1D33 -- it's an audio, excuse me. If we can play this, and then we can ask this series of questions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: " ... said that this would be a great tragedy because we know that many of the Serbs who live there would leave, probably most of them. There would, of course, be thousands of dead on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that's just obviously a snippet of that, Mr. Ambassador, but taking this all -- obviously there are other aspects or comments along this regard. You had concluded at that time that if any type of military activity was conducted that Martic would get -- or the Krajina Serbs would leave the area, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had concluded that the Krajina Serbs would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you base that on, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I based it on the fact that most of the Krajina Serbs -- most of the Serbs in Western Slavonia had left after Operation Flash; I based it on -- what I would -- a well-founded fear of what Croatian military action might mean based on the experience in the Medak pocket; I based it on the attitude that Tudjman had toward the Serb population; and I based it very much on the vehement anti-Croat -- or Croatia and anti-Croat propaganda of the Serb leadership, which equated Tudjman's Croatia inaccurately, equated Tudjman's Croatia with the Ustasha regime of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this was on the heels of this Operation Flash in Western Slavonia where you said that the Croats acted to their credit and that the -- was an element of Serbs who actually stayed, and some of those Serbs thereafter decided they were going to leave anyway.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think of the 3.000 who decided to stay, that they in fact remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the day that Operation Storm was going to commence -- well, let's even go before that. Let's go to paragraph 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the audio which was just played, do you intend to tender that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I will tender it at this time, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also tell us -- I saw that it's audio, not video, but I saw on the screen three names, one of the three perhaps the person who spoke. I've got no idea what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a -- that was -- the only person that was speaking was the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I can't -- and in what context was this audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was on the 3rd of August, 1995. It was actually the last meeting that the ambassador had with President Tudjman prior to Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now that's clear to me. Mr. Tieger, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless there is something different about this clip that I don't know about. This is a small audio clip of a transcript -- transcripts that were -- a transcript, excuse me, that was tendered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and admitted. Is it part of the transcripts of at least now the audio of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the audio add anything to what is on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would have to check, Your Honour, but we gave the Prosecution the entire audio from the 3rd meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the issue. The question is whether it adds to the evidence already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would have to go back and check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, let's then refrain at this moment from giving it a number. If it is the same, then I think there's no need to hear it again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Galbraith. I'm sorry. There are 25 people in this courtroom, so sometimes I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The title on that audio was -- included Holbrooke's name, and I have no idea why it was included because he was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Neither have I, Mr. Galbraith, so therefore -- Mr. Kehoe, if you would please check the matter and see whether there is any need to tender it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a mistake on Holbrooke. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ambassador. Now, Mr. Ambassador, by the way, with regard to going back to Western Slavonia, there was a percentage of the Serb population that left Western Slavonia even though the operation by the HV, in your words, brought them credit. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leaving aside your characterization, there was -- there were about 3.000 -- which I explained my view of, but there were 3.000 of the roughly 13.000 people in Western Slavonia stayed, the 10.000 who left, I think, most of them left actually before the Croatians took over the area, so they left in fear of what would happen rather than leaving -- I mean, some part of them may have left after the Croatians arrived, but some of them were also simply fleeing what they feared would be the -- what the Croatians might do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was that percentage that did in fact stay?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to -- to paragraph 81. You note in the first sentence: "I don't think it was Tudjman's plan to expel all Serbs from Croatia." Now -- do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned to us that when you were talking to President Tudjman you were not giving him a red light or a yellow light or a green light. You were just passing on your concerns. It's a fact, Mr. Ambassador, that if you thought that President Tudjman was ordering the start of Operation Storm to expel all the Serbs from the Krajina, you would have given him a red light as you did back in November of 1994, wouldn't you? And I mean "you," I mean the United States government.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, when we gave him a red light back in November of 1994 it had nothing -- it was not because we thought he was going to expel the Serbs. We gave it for -- the reason we gave the red light is that we feared it would lead to a wider war. Second, yes -- well, it's a hypothetical question which I can't answer, but I can answer for myself, which is that if we had believed that -- if I had believed that Tudjman was going to expel all the Serbs from the Krajina, I would have urged in the strongest possible way for my government to give a red light to this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you didn't give any such urging to your government to give a red light, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not believe that Tudjman was going to expel the Serbs. As noted, I believed that most of them would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek here clarification, Mr. Kehoe, because you introduce in your question, if you thought that President Tudjman was ordering the start of Operation Storm to expel all the Serbs from the Krajina, there is an implicit assumption that that was the purpose. First of all, Mr. Galbraith, did you consider the purpose of Operation Storm primarily to expel the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you consider that this was or could be a side effect of militarily taking over the Krajina territory and have it within Croatia again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not consider that the expulsion of the Serbs would be a side effect, but I did consider that the departure of the Serbs would be a side effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you earlier answered already some questions about whether that suited President Tudjman or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did answer those questions, and -- and to state briefly, I believe that the departure of the Serbs was something that he wanted -- he was happy to see happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But to follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, usually if you mix up things, if you then -- you might not -- that you might get answers which do not -- which respond primarily to the mixing up of elements rather than to have a clear analysis of what the witnesses wants to tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, to follow up on Judge Orie's question just, it goes back to your first line in paragraph 81. You did not think that when Operation Storm was commencing on the 4th of August that the plan was to expel the Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That question has put and answered. Clearly, there is a clear answer on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think based on the answer to the question that you gave that -- I just come back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that was not what was intended by Operation Storm to achieve, isn't it, Mr. Galbraith? That's how I understood your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm getting confused with all the double negatives here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think Operation Storm was undertaken for the purpose of expelling the Serbs from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can just change subjects to -- to after Operation Storm and -- after Operation Storm, activities continued against the Serbs shortly after Operation Storm. Were you aware of that? I'm talking about the HV against the Bosnian Serbs in conjunction with the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that operations continued after Operation Storm and -- but to go with your colleague, they were undertaken in conjunction with the government of -- the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, which ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me stay with the preposition that the fighting with the HV against the Bosnian Serbs and to that extent the elements of the ARSK that were with them, that continued almost immediately after the end of Operation Storm, did it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army continued its military campaign. Having taken over the Krajina, it continued its military campaign into Bosnia, fighting the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And going back to your diary at August the 7th, page 36, the second paragraph, in the middle of that paragraph: "Croatia's actions were welcomed by many in Washington because of its implications for Bosnia." Now, who was it in Washington that welcomed Croatia's actions?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people in Washington welcomed Croatia's actions, and it was certainly welcomed by the -- by many in the Clinton Administration for the reason that I stated, which is that it began to change the situation in Bosnia. Ambassador Holbrooke, for example, has written in his book "To End A War" that this action was the turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The turning point --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the war, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- it led to the defeat of the Bosnian Serbs. The map changed from being one in which the Serbs held 70 per cent of Bosnia and the federation, 30, to one whereby October of 1995 the federation held, I don't know, 54, 55 per cent and frankly, once the federation held 55 per cent it was a lot easier to get to a 51/49 arrangement than it was when the Serbs held 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And so as earlier as August the 7th, there was the -- certainly your thought that this activity by the HV ultimately in conjunction with the ABiH would continue on into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my thought that that would occur, it was my hope that that would occur, and that was my recommendation to my government that we not take any action that would discourage Croatia from continuing with that campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that the HV on the command of General Gotovina was largely responsible for changing the map in Bosnia to bring about the Dayton Peace talks?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army military campaign in Bosnia, along with the military campaign by the army of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina along with NATO air-strikes that began at the very end of August were the three element -- decisive elements that led to the end of the Bosnia war, and it would not have been -- it would not have happened if it were not for the Croatian army's military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will continue on. I don't know if Your Honour wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is time for a break. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may start your remaining two hours and one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But who's counting, right, Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, as the offensive with the ABiH and the HV moved against the Serbs, it -- and moving through Bosnia, you kept abreast of what was going on, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you knew, for instance, about Operation Mistral and that portion of the offensive against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And throughout this -- and let me direct your -- if I could direct you to your diary on September the 15th at page 54. If you could go to the last paragraph of September 15th on 54, you see right above the September 16th. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, the authorities for the Republic of Croatia in this instance, Minister Susak, asked you -- it notes that Susak pressed me as to how far they could go including the Banja Luka question. So they were actually consulting the United States authorities as to how far they should push the Bosnian Serbs back, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take this further, and I want to let you hear an audio from 1 October 1995, 1D33-0081.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Audio of what, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. This is 1 October 1995. This is the audio. President Tudjman is on it. The ambassador is there, Ambassador Holbrooke as well. It's actually two audios, but this is the first of two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "... say it is very possible, therefore, that we could have a cease-fire within a week if we want one, and I would urge you to achieve whatever you can militarily in the next week because the pressure for cease-fires is -- "Excuse me, would you be so kind ... "I would urge you to do whatever you can militarily in the next week in western Bosnia. In other words, in other words, you may have a cease-fire within one week or less, and I would hope that you could take Sanski Most and Prijedor and Bosanski Nova if possible before a cease-fire. If you take -- if you take those three towns before a cease-fire, we can have a successful negotiation on the map. In any case, officially, the United States always says no more military action, but privately, and I cannot be quoted on this, I would urge you to consider the fact that the pressure for a cease-fire within the next week is very, very high. And once we have a cease-fire, I think it will be very important to create a situation in which refugees can return and -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we ask some questions about that, Mr. Ambassador, I just want to let you play another clip of that meeting on 1 October, 1995. 1D33-0082.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "... so let there be no misunderstanding about this famous question of American red lights, green lights, and so on because you read a lot of things in the press. My position has always been clear: Banja Luka was a Serb city and would remain Serb after the negotiations. Why create a half -- a quarter of a million refugees or 200.000 refugees? But I never said not to take Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, on these offensives going into western Bosnia, the Croatian authorities were taking the guidance from the United States via Ambassador Holbrooke on what towns to take so they could move towards a final settlement of the matter in the former Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Holbrooke and I had private discussions with the Croatians about the military situation, and we did offer our thoughts as to what towns should be taken, and I think we felt strongly that Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi should be part of the Federation. And we had discussions and debates about some other places, including Banja Luka, and I'm not entirely sure looking back now that we necessarily made the right call. But as Ambassador Holbrooke said in that exchange, the -- that was a little different from the official view of the Administration which was that we wanted -- that the military operations should cease. I suppose it's fair to say that the United States government does not always operate in perfect harmony. I also do not think that we were in the business of micromanaging, and we did not want to be in the business of micromanaging Croatian military operations or directing them, but we were offering our views as to -- on -- on issues that were both a matter of justice because Prijedor was more or less the Auschwitz of Bosnia and on places that also would make it possible to achieve a peace settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it's fair to say, Mr. Ambassador, that Ambassador Holbrooke when you were present was encouraging and further pushing further military actions of the HV to take certain towns, including Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've played the tape. I think it speaks for itself, and I think I've given you what our view was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the HV did take Sanski Most, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And throughout all this, the purpose of a discussion with the Croatian authorities was to engage in military campaigns to defeat the Bosnian Serbs and bring people to a negotiating table, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to defeat the Bosnian Serbs who had -- had committed genocide. It was to liberate, and I use that term, liberate territory in which Bosniaks and Croats had lived from which they had been brutally expelled, Prijedor was a predominantly Bosniak town, and to make possible -- to have enough change in the military situation to make possible a peace settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which ultimately was concluded at the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concluded about 50 days after -- 51 days after the message that you just played ending a war that had lasted four years, more than four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when there was an expression by Ambassador Holbrooke not to take Banja Luka, Banja Luka wasn't taken?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka was not taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, throughout all this, Mr. Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, by October 1, I don't think that -- Banja Luka was really on the table anymore. The decisive moment for that was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But through all this as these offensives are moving forward, the person who is occupied with these offensives on the ground into western Bosnia is General Gotovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't -- it was the -- as far as I was concerned it was the Croatian military. I'm not going to comment on the role of General Gotovina. I'm not saying that's wrong in any way. It's just after all these years the specifics of that are not all that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could just go back for a second to, again, where we just read for Susak asking how far they could go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is it your intention to tender the audiotapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will tender 1D33-00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it seems that you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, with regard to the putting of this tape together, Mr. Misetic would like to inform the court of a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interest of complete disclosure into the Prosecution, the tapes we played, the clips were -- we cut some of the discussion because otherwise the clip would have gone on for ten minutes. I think it would be appropriate since the Prosecution has the complete audio if they can get some time if they have any objection to the fact that the audios had been cut. If -- you know, they may find -- they may have an objection to it, so before we tender them into evidence they should be given an opportunity on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and I was wondering if there are not transcripts that were prepared in connection with this as opposed to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And especially who says what because what we see on our screen, I have been listening. It gives the text, but if Mr. Galbraith says that Mr. Holbrooke is speaking, I take it that he is, but on the transcript you usually indicate who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is our error, then, Your Honour. If necessary, we will clear it up, but it was Mr. Holbrooke that was speaking on the audio. I believe the Prosecution has been given a transcript of the complete segment prior to the cut, and that would have been this afternoon at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will then delay both tendering and taking any decisions on admission until tomorrow. Mr. Tieger, is that sufficient time for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour, and try to accommodate that time. If there is any problem, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best -- okay. If I -- no, no, I see the point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, the actual transcript, the ones that -- the excerpts that we played does have the identity of the people that are talking, so I -- we will provide that for guidance from -- to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the individual that was just talking on those tapes, October 1st, that was Ambassador Holbrooke, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just going back to General Gotovina, if you see the -- again, towards the carry-over paragraph on September 15th, you do mention a meeting between Gotovina and the 5th and 7th Corps commanders. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is on September 15, just before the inclusion of the September 16th entry.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So at least then you were aware of the fact that General Gotovina was the HV commander who was out fighting these battles?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I know that General Gotovina was the HV commander. The only reason I am reluctant to comment is that at this point I don't remember what dates he might have, been where, and, you know, what his exact responsibilities are, and I know that's an issue in this case, and I know there are people who are just going to be better able to testify about that than I do. But I certainly do know of his role in leading the Croatian forces into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate your concern. If I can just shift gears to yet another topic that you talked about on direct, Mr. Ambassador. And following up on your mentioning that General Gotovina was in Bosnia conducting activities with the HV, I'd like to take you back to Knin and talk a bit about what was happening back in the Knin area while matters are moving ahead in other military theatres, and at the first juncture I'd just like to play you - for the sake of speed, Mr. Ambassador - a video along with an audio, and if we can start with this video first of the 8th of August, 1995. It is it ID 330091. It is of Mr. Jarnjak in Zagreb as you will see -- excuse me, 1D33-0090, and I'm sure you knew that Mr. Jarnjak was the minister of the interior. And if we can just play this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Good evening. I hereby open this conversation and welcome the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak. "Mr. Ivan Jarnjak: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. Allow me to inform you about what the Ministry of Interior is doing and will be doing in the areas that are now being liberated. The constitutional and legal order of the Republic of Croatia is being introduced in the newly liberated areas. To do that, it is necessary for the Ministry of the Interior along with other institutions to enter those areas with its forces. Following the Croatian army and the special units of the Ministry of Interior, the civilian police entered those areas, as well, immediately after them, establishing fundamental police and border police stations. Following the guidelines of state policy back in 1992, the Ministry of Interior developed the organisational structure of two police administration and police stations for the entire Republic of Croatia, including the territories that have now been liberated. Thus, we've had the entire organisational structure ready since 1992, and now we are merely implementing it. Of the police stations that had been expelled from their areas during the aggression, those police stations that had been expelled in 1991 and partly in 1992 continued operating in the areas where they had been relocated. Now they return to their original areas, those being the police spaces Lovinac, Drnis, Vrlika, Kijevo, Slunj, Petrinja, Glina, and Hrvatska Kostajnica. The expelled police stations have also been returned, those being Cetingrad, Saborsko, Plaski, and Lasinje. The border police have become operational in Hrvatska Kostajnica, Kijevo, Slunj, Donji Lapac, Strmica, Donji Srb, and Licko Petrovo Selo. Police stations are prepared to receive the border police in Dvor and Topusko. "According to the constitutional law on human rights and liberties, the rights of ethnic communities and minorities, police administrations which must be organised according to these laws have become operational. They are the Knin police administration and the Glina police administration. Those are districts according to this constitutional law which have special statutes. In those area, of course, police stations have also been established for Knin, Donji Lapac, Gracac, Korenica, Benkovac, and Obrovac. These are the police stations which form part of this police administration. "For the district of Glina, the police administration has been established with the police stations of Glina, Vojnic, and Hrvatska Kostajnica. The police stations the Vrgin Most and Dvor are ready to go back to their areas of operation. Immediately after the Croatian army and the special police of the Ministry of the Interior completed the first part of their task and the combat operations and activities ceased, members of the Ministry of the Interior entered the populated localities and started securing the populated localities and the communications connecting those localities and controlling and directing the traffic. Concurrently with the establishment of the police stations and the police substations, all services of the Ministry of the Interior became operational as well. That means the civilian protection, the fire-fighters have become operational, and also preconditions are being created for the establishment of services that conduct civil affairs, that is issuing Croatian documents. "The civil protection units commenced the sanitation activities in the field, disposition of small livestock and cattle, taking care of the abandoned moveable property, and any real estate left behind, first in the settled areas and in the following days it shall begin also in the non-populated areas, probably over the next couple of days. To all those residing in the newly liberated areas, to those who remained, and to those who will return, that is the displaced persons, we guarantee personal safety, safety of their property, and we guarantee public law and order. Thank you very much." "Thank you, Minister Jarnjak."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if I could move to an audio on this score, Mr. Ambassador, from the 19th of October with you, Ambassador Holbrooke, and President Tudjman, and this is President Tudjman speaking -- excuse me. No, it's Mr. -- yeah. This is 1D33-0474.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The third item is related, is the question of what's going on in western Bosnia and the Krajina, and this is sometimes called by the press a human rights problem, but it's really much, much more than that. It's a political problem. It's a problem for the image of Croatia -- "Did you hear the -- information from my [indiscernible] yesterday? "Press conference. There was a press conference by Mr. Jarnjak yesterday. "No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our Ministry of Internal Affairs notified -- do you have the information?" Tudjman speaking ... "... figures will be.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They clarified -- they elucidated 40 murders and turned over to court 13 perpetrators. "13 persons have been taken into custody and -- "Oh, yes. I did see that. I didn't know it was your minister.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Among them were Serbs. "There were also criminals as well as drug addicts among them. And out of 800 or something cases of looting, 619 had already been clarified in terms of investigation. More than one. And certainly the number of kills was not 100 plus as was reported; moreover some of these killings took place within the scope of military operations, but as I said, only 41 killings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And the minister stated that he received orders from me to take steps immediately during the operation to prevent all conduct of this kind."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last item, if I may, Mr. Ambassador, before we go into this area, and that is from P -- again P451. It is your book, your -- your press conference with Secretary Shattuck of the 30th of September, 1995. And this would be page 06069735. And if you could go to -- again, the second page of that and not the carry-over paragraph but the second paragraph where it says: "Second," at the top. If we could just blow that up a bit. Maybe just move ahead. You have a copy of that before you, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. And talking about the abuses. "Second, these abuses need not have occurred on this scale if the Croatian government had taken measures to prevent them, such as by arresting and prosecuting the perpetrators, those who are guilty of these crimes and by deploying civilian police rapidly enough to keep order in the period immediately after the military actions. The Croatian officials with whom I met assured me that steps are now being taken to address the security situation and the human rights abuses and crimes that have occurred." Now, if I may, the first video of Minister Jarnjak was the 8th of August, 1995, and on the 9th of August, you called for his firing, so you were aware of Minister Jarnjak and what his role was, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you talk about that in your diary, in your discussions on the 10th of August. And you were aware that -- certainly as a result of your conversations on the 19th of October that President Tudjman had told Jarnjak to solve these problems down in the Krajina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of the conversations on October 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, during the course of the conversations on the 19th, President Tudjman told you and Ambassador Holbrooke that he had told Jarnjak that -- solve these problems down in the Krajina that had come up after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's what is in the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I don't want to speak for you or Ambassador Shattuck, but in this press conference you note -- maybe it's Ambassador Shattuck that notes that civilian police -- they didn't deploy civilian police rapidly enough. Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was a fact, I mean, that they -- in your view and Ambassador -- Secretary Shattuck's view is they didn't get enough police down there quick enough to ensure that this activity didn't go on. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to speak for Secretary Shattuck. That is it -- that is it not my view of the problem. My view of the problem is that the personnel that there were did not and I believe there was no desire for them to prevent the looting and burning and killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, if I may offer into evidence first the video, 1D33-0090, and then the audio, 1D33-0474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First the video. Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection to the video, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D411 is admitted into evidence. Then the audio. I think we played several portions or was it just one portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was just one, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could take the same -- if we could take the same approach to this audio as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, that we do not yet assign a number. I think that is what we did the previous ones, and you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- same best to give a response by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And same question again, if there is an transcript available of that audio...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I slowly start recognizing the voice, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is a transcript that was given to the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And to clarify, the individuals who were talking on that tape, the American voice was Ambassador Holbrooke, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the other individual talking in Croatian was President Tudjman and his translator. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was talking in English and Croatian, and then, of course, it was his translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, with regard to -- to the activities of the Ministry of Defence, do you know what steps the Ministry of Defence were doing to control this activity?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, since I don't believe it was controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the Ministry of the Interior? Do you know what the Ministry of the Interior was doing to control this activity?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- if I can answer the question what was the Ministry of the Interior doing, the -- what Minister Jarnjak described in that press conference was accurate, that is, the Croatian government had police and indeed the entire municipal governments there in place, I guess, since 1992, but they certainly were ready to deploy, and I saw them deploying within hours when I was in Petrinja, so they were deploying people into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But with regard to investigations or pursuing cases, and I'm talking about the Ministry of the Interior, you don't know what they were doing? You don't know how many cases they were investigating; you don't know how many cases were prosecuted, nothing?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I certainly had some idea of it, but I felt that -- we believed that only a small part -- number of the cases were actually prosecuted, and what President Tudjman explained in that audiotape, that -- it was criminals, drug addicts, and Serbs who were doing it was in my view an absurd and untrue explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador -- I will take a break. During the course of your consultations with the various officials of the Republic of Croatia, be it Minister Susak in the Defence or Minister Jarnjak in the Ministry of the Interior, did they make you aware of orders that were being given and instructions that were being given and discussions that were going on to get these issues in the Krajina under control?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly Minister Susak and I discussed this. But the issue, again, was not what orders were being issued or what orders I was told was being issued. It was what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, my question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of one of your previous answers, which appears to me -- You were earlier asked about the activities of the Ministry of Defence, whether you knew what steps the Ministry of Defence were doing to control this activity. Your answer was: "No, since I don't believe it was controlled." Now, whether something is controlled seems to be the result of possible efforts. Linking the "no" to "since there was no control" leaves me with the puzzle whether you were aware of any activities, whether effective or not, and this seems to be the same issue as touched upon by the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not a question of whether the activities were effective or not. It is whether the activities were intended to control or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first in factual terms describe whether you were aware of any activities, and then we could go on and to see whether these activities were an effort. An effort to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly at the time, I was aware of activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to be -- I mean, it's been some time, so the -- this included, as I recall, the deployment of police - of course that would be interior - promises that -- that they -- that efforts would be made to stop the looting; promises to prosecute people; promises to secure areas. These were the kinds of promises that were made to me by the Croatians as I raised the question of what was going on in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Ambassador, were you aware of orders either by the minister of the interior or the Ministry of Defence to make all efforts to curtail criminal activity in the Krajina? Were you aware of those orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's try to get it step by step, first of all, whether there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you are -- orders and then you mention two ministries, and you also say that the orders were to make all efforts. Let's first see whether Mr. Galbraith is aware of orders given, first of all, by the ministry or minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- I'm sure I was told that the Ministry of the Interior had given orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what these orders were about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sure I knew in more detail in 1995 than I do now, but the general thrust of it would be the -- would be to secure the area to -- to arrest perpetrators to stop the illegal activity that the I was -- that the US government was complaining about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was true for the orders from both the ministries you learned about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would have been the thrust of both the orders. As to the specifics of what each ministry was doing, I don't at this point recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I know that you didn't see that that -- there was a curtailment on the ground, but, Mr. Ambassador, if orders were being given to stop criminal activities in the Krajina, then permitting these criminal activities was not state policy, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make my answer a bit more precise. I was told that orders were given by these ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can take that just one step further. If you were told and if in fact there were such orders - and are in evidence, Your Honour - if there were in fact such orders, then the burning of these residences that you discussed on your direct would not be state policy, would it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with -- with what you've just stated. I have enough experience over the years that I served in Croatia with Croatian officials and Serb officials, giving orders and saying they'd given orders that they had -- and making promises that they had no intention of keeping, and I do not believe that the Croatian government made a serious attempt to bring this destruction under control until such time as it was basically -- there was nothing left for the Serbs to return to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So dealing with your last answer on if these orders were given, if these orders were given to cease this activity by either the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of Interior, those orders would have been given contrary to state policy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
