utterances.text: I don't -- I do not believe that the -- that the -- the orders that I was told about were -- constituted a serious effort to -- to bring this violence and destruction to an end because I believe that the top Croatian leadership wanted Serb property to be destroyed so that -- that -- there would be no possibility of Serbs -- of significant number of Serbs returning. I believe that was their -- their policy, and -- so that the orders -- that is the context in which I -- I saw these orders, and that's really what I can testify to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you knew Minister Susak, and you knew Minister Jarnjak. Is it your testimony that Minister Jarnjak and Minister Susak would issue orders contrary to Tudjman's wishes? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me to assume that the orders constituted a sincere effort to bring this to an end, and certainly in -- at the time that much of this destruction was taking place, I suppose, mid-August/September, I do not think that the Croatian state authorities wanted this violence brought to an end probably by October, once it had -- everything that -- so much had already been destroyed, then, yes, and there was so much criticism, probably they did want it brought to an end. But you know, that is my -- my statement, and it is very hard for me to get into what -- which almost seems Mr. Kehoe, to be semantics here. My point is, and I believe this, and I -- it comes from very extensive observation of -- on my own part at the reporting of the embassy and lots of other sources that the destruction that took place was something that Croatia could have prevented, chose not to prevent because it served the purposes of the top Croatian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ambassador, I asked you the question on line 18 of page 89: "Is it your testimony that Minister Jarnjak and Minister Susak would issue orders contrary to Tudjman's wishes? Yes or no." Let me ask this question: Did you ever know of Minister Susak or Minister Jarnjak issuing orders contrary to Tudjman's wishes, ever?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to the comment that you were talking about about the burnings and preventing burnings -- to prevent people from returning. Now, you mentioned to us in your testimony earlier today that there was some 2 to 300.000 Croatian displaced people within Croatia. Is that approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someplace in that range. I mean, 150.000 to 300.000. I can't pull the figure out of the air right now, but there were a significant number of Croatian towns within the Krajina, and of course there were a lot of people from Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we also had the displaced people -- well, then they were refugees from Bosnia that were also in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were Bosnian Croats who were not refugees but who came to Croatia, as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your diary at -- on September the 15th at the bottom of page 52. Do you see that, sir? And we're talking at the bottom of that page --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said: "I also noted that not many would want to return." What we're talking about is Krajina Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "At most, 20 per cent. Using his own low-ball figures for the number of refugees, I pointed out that this would be fewer than 20 per cent and Croatia could clearly absorb that." Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a small correction. The diary doesn't say 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 20.000. Excuse me. 20.000. I'm sorry. "Fewer than 20.000 and Croatia could surely absorb that." And the 20.000 is 20 per cent, obviously, of the 100.000 refugees or displaced people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, while this burning and looting is going on, Mr. Ambassador, we have -- we talked about somewhere, 150, 200.000, however many Croatian displaced people there were within Croatia, that needed housing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at this point -- these people had been displaced in 1991, so by 1995 they were they were all housed. Just to come back to the previous question. That figure 20.000 is using Sarinic's low figure for the number of Serbs who had left. I -- I believed -- we believed that the number who left -- that left was more. I think we think it was about 180.000. But since Sarinic had said it was 20 -- it was 100.000, then I -- and that 20 per cent might return, I then -- that's where the 20.000 -- I'm reporting on a conversation I had with Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, hadn't Tudjman told you previously that 100.000 had left and that he said only 10 per cent were going to return and you said 20 per cent would return? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman had said in one meeting that 10 per cent would return, but our belief was that the number that had left was about 180.000 as I recall. But here, you see, I'm -- I'm making an argument to Sarinic in my role as a mediator. He's telling me 100.000 people have left, so I say, okay, what's the big deal if 20 per cent return? I'm accepting for that -- because it is going to be more persuasive to Sarinic if I say that' it's 20 per cent of 100.000 will return. Okay, that's your figure. Then if I say, no, no, we believe the figure's 180.000, and therefore 36.000 will return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But our principle, our principle is we wanted everybody to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Let us turn to P455, which is a Prosecutor's transcript of 10 August 1995, and this is an interview -- or excuse me, a meeting which you participated in with President Tudjman. I'm not sure you have that, Mr. Ambassador, but if you do, I gladly invite you to go to page 3 of -- it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of this -- the third page in, and this is President Tudjman talking at the top of the page. He tells you on 10 August 1995 -- oops, excuse me. Can we go to the -- the pagination you received is a little bit different. If we can go to the prior page in the English. Go to the bottom of that page, please. He notes: "On the 10th of August, 1995, in certain moment we had over 400.000 refugees from" -- Go to the next page. -- "the Croat area." Goes to the top of the next page, if we can ... Now, Ambassador, whether it's 400 refugees, 300 refugees, 200.000 -- excuse me, 200.000, 300.000, 400.000 refugees, there was a serious housing problem in Croatia after Operation Storm, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the serious housing problem in Croatia took place in 1991, really, and incidentally the 400.000 figure -- there were people who were dislocated because of the fighting in 1991 who were in 1991 able to return to their homes because there was -- there was more or less a cease-fire, and also the Croatians re-took some areas that had been taken by the JNA in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ambassador, did you not know of the serious housing problem for refugees in Croatia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was a problem that was created in 1991 but, yes, it certainly existed in 1995. I just testified that there were -- about people being in the hotels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And given these hundreds of thousands of people that were looking for places to live, is it still your position that it was the state policy of the Republic of Croatia to burn down houses that they needed to put people in to live?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the policy of the top Croatian leadership. That is -- that is what I have testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are beyond 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, we adjourn. But have I one puzzle on my mind, Mr. Galbraith. I'm not asking you to answer the question now, but today we talked about this 10 per cent, and we learned from you that 10 per cent is -- 10.000 is 10 percent of from 100.000. Yesterday, the issue was raised in the context of what the goals were, and you then answered that you would first like to make the point that Tudjman, when really pressed, spoke about, you know, maybe 10 percent of the Serb population being there. Today, the same issue was raised, but now it was -- it looked more as would they return? That seems to be an expectation rather than a goal set. It was unclear to me whether, when talking about the 10.000, the 10 per cent, whether you meant as I understood more or less yesterday to be the goal or not more than 10 per cent being the goal, or whether it was a realistic expectation as it appeared to be more from your text today. If you could think that over overnight, and we can adjourn for the day. We adjourn until tomorrow morning -- no, I got my note but ... 9.00 in the morning, Mr. Galbraith, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
